models.name: Flux
models.notes: Natural-language prose works best; no negative prompt — phrase exclusions positively (say 'clear sky', not 'no clouds').

models.name: Higgsfield (MCSLA)
models.notes: MCSLA = Model, Camera, Subject, Look, Action. Under ~200 words. One primary camera move per shot. Prefer positive phrasing over negations.

models.name: Midjourney
models.notes: Comma-separated phrases, subject first. Parameters go last. Verify the current --v value and parameters in Midjourney docs.

models.name: Stable Diffusion / SDXL
models.notes: Tag-style prompt plus a separate negative prompt. Weighting syntax such as (word:1.2) is UI-dependent (A1111/ComfyUI).

models.name: Seedance 2.0
models.notes: Order follows the creator handover guide: duration/shot type, location, character, action, camera, timing, lighting, audio, performance, style, restrictions. Describe physical actions, not feelings.

entries.title: Raghav Whiskey Sequence 15s
entries.notes: Product/detail → character reveal → information/reaction. Tells the model event order, camera move, what is sharp vs blurred, the dialogue and the exact reaction.
entries.body:
15-second continuous sequence with three connected shots.

SHOT 1 — 0-5 seconds

Extreme macro close-up of a crystal whiskey tumbler on a polished walnut desk. Two clear ice cubes fall into the empty glass in slow motion. A rich amber stream of whiskey pours over the ice, creating small ripples and bubbles. The camera slowly moves in a circular orbit around the glass. Warm amber light reflects naturally through the crystal. Premium, realistic materials and reflections.

SHOT 2 — 5-10 seconds

The camera smoothly moves upward with the whiskey glass as Raghav's hand lifts it from the desk. Keep the glass sharp in the foreground. Raghav's face stays softly out of focus in the background. As the glass reaches his lips, gradually shift focus to Raghav's side profile. He takes one slow sip. The glass partially covers his face.

SHOT 3 — 10-15 seconds

The whiskey glass slowly lowers into the foreground. Keep Raghav's side profile sharp and the background heavily blurred. A person remains out of focus in the background and says:

"Sir..... ...naya IPS officer aa chuka hai."

Raghav does not turn. He pauses for a moment. Then the corner of his lips slowly rises into a confident smile. Hold on his smile.

Keep the same character, location, lighting and glass throughout the sequence. Realistic human movement, realistic liquid and glass physics, natural focus changes. No extra characters visible in focus. No exaggerated acting. No cartoon look.

entries.body: A courier in a reflective jacket walks toward the camera down a rain-soaked neon alley at night, puddles mirroring magenta and cyan signs, steam rising from grates. The camera tracks backward at the same pace, handheld with subtle sway. Shallow depth of field, anamorphic flares. Rain, distant traffic, soft synth hum.

Natural skin texture. Subtle handheld breathing. No exaggerated acting.

entries.title: 15-Second Block Structure
entries.body:
Beginning — where the camera and characters are at the start
Main action — the most important thing that happens
End — a clear final state that can connect to the next shot

If a block contains too many unrelated actions, divide the story into more shots. Give the model a sequence it can actually execute.

entries.title: Camera Matches Emotion
entries.body:
Anger / tension → jittery handheld, small irregular micro-twitches, no stabiliser
Calm / control → smooth handheld breathing, steady rhythm
Sadness / vulnerability → slow, low handheld, slight downward drift
Shock / revelation → static, sharp freeze, then very slow push-in or pull-out
Action → 60fps, 180° shutter, clean motion blur
Final beat / verdict → top-shot freeze, 0.3-0.5s
Emotional breakdown → slow pull-back from close to wide ("leave the character alone")

If the emotion changes within a take, write named phases and change the camera with it.

entries.title: Casting Lock Table
entries.body:
Before generating many scenes, lock each recurring character's:
- Face — the same person stays recognisable
- Hair — changes make the character feel different
- Skin tone — keeps the character consistent
- Body / proportions — prevents shape drift
- Costume foundation — a consistent base look
- Overall appearance — one clear reference for the show

For recurring characters the reference image is the identity anchor.

entries.title: Choosing the Shot by Story Need
entries.body:
Ask: "If I could not use words here, what would I show the audience?"

Where we are → wide or aerial establishing shot
Who is with whom → two-shot / medium shot
A character's reaction → close-up
A specific object or clue → detail / insert shot
Someone travelling → vehicle / movement shot
A reveal → controlled camera move, or a shot that hides then reveals
A change in perspective → POV / inside-vehicle / over-the-shoulder

These are ways of thinking about what information the viewer needs, not rules.

entries.title: Common Beginner Mistakes
entries.body:
- Starting with a prompt before understanding the scene.
- Trying to make every shot spectacular instead of readable.
- Changing a character's face because one generation looks nicer.
- Putting several unrelated actions into one shot.
- Vague instructions ("make it emotional") without describing what the person does.
- Saying "cinematic" without explaining the actual camera.
- Adding random background characters or objects.
- Changing a recurring location from shot to shot.
- Trying to fix five problems at the same time.
- Keeping a beautiful shot that tells the story incorrectly.

entries.title: Continuity Check After Every Generation
entries.body:
Character — same face, hair, body, overall appearance
Costume — matches the script and nearby shots
Location — still feels like the same place
Lighting — makes sense for the scene and time
Props — important objects stay consistent
Position — the action makes sense from the previous shot
Story — the shot communicates the intended beat
Performance — the intended level of emotion
Physics — bodies and objects move naturally

entries.title: Devgarh Sequence Shot Logic
entries.body:
1. Establish the world — wide establishing view (location, scale, weather, time)
2. World → people — character-focused view
3. Show the relationship — two-character interaction
4. Use movement to connect locations — vehicle / transition
5. Change the point of view — interior vehicle view
6. Let ordinary details build the location — rural location
7. Give the important face attention — close-up
8. Establish the room before the emotional close-up — room / situation
9. Let the face carry the tension — emotional close-up (or: objects tell the story, overhead)
10. Show an important object clearly — detail / evidence
11. Give a small physical action its own moment — action detail
12. Return to the character's perspective — interior character view

Each shot is chosen for what it communicates, not only because it looks good.

entries.title: Edit the Story
entries.body:
- Choose the take that communicates the story best.
- Wide shots establish place and relationships.
- Close-ups when the audience needs to notice a face or reaction.
- Detail shots when an object or clue matters.
- Movement shots connect locations or create transitions.
- Dialogue, ambience and music connect the visual pieces.
- Remove shots that look good but slow down or confuse the story.

Viewer test: do I understand what is happening? Do I know where I am? Do I know who matters? Do I know what to notice?

entries.title: Fix the Specific Problem
entries.body:
Wrong face → strengthen the character reference / identity instruction
Wrong costume → make the costume requirement clearer
Wrong action → simplify the action and describe the sequence
Wrong camera → describe the starting position and exact movement
Object moves incorrectly → describe cause → direction → contact → final position
Too many people / objects → remove them and explicitly say no extra characters/objects
Too much acting → tell the character to stay calm, subtle or serious
Looks too artificial → improve natural materials, lighting, depth and physical behaviour
Shot doesn't tell the story → go back to the script and reconsider what needs to be shown

Change one thing at a time.

entries.title: Hero Frame First
entries.body:
1. Generate 5-10 cheap image variations; pick the closest.
2. Refine that one image (inpaint / edit) until it is exactly right.
3. Animate ONCE from the approved hero frame.

Spend more on cheap image generations, far less on expensive video re-rolls. Change one variable at a time between generations.

entries.title: Keep the Language Physical
entries.body:
Models respond to what a person, camera or object actually does.
"He looks powerful" is weak. Describe posture, expression, movement and framing instead: "He sits upright, shoulders square, chin level, eyes steady on the door; the camera is low and slowly pushes in."

Replace: "make it emotional" → what the person's face and body do. "Cinematic" → the actual camera.

entries.title: Keep the World Consistent
entries.body:
- Identify recurring locations.
- Identify important vehicles and objects.
- Keep the visual language of recurring places consistent.
- If the story has a specific time of day, keep the lighting believable across nearby shots.
- Only change a location when the story says the location has changed.

A consistent character in a house, road or vehicle that changes every shot still feels wrong.

entries.title: Make the Visual, Not a Storyboard
entries.body:
Traditional storyboard → my process
Draw the shot → visualise the shot in words
Lock the drawing → generate the visual
Adjust the drawing → adjust the prompt / reference
Shoot from the drawing → use the approved visual as the target for the video generation

A generated frame is easier for non-filmmakers to understand than a sketch.

entries.title: One-Move Camera Rule
entries.body:
Specify ONE primary camera move per shot. Stacking moves (dolly + pan + tilt) is the leading cause of jitter, unwanted rotation and failed generations.

Wrong: "dolly push forward while panning left and tilting up to reveal the skyline"
Right: "slow dolly push from medium shot to tight close-up over 8 seconds"

Need several moves? Split into separate shots, or state a timed sequence ("pans left 0-3s, holds, pushes in 4-8s").

entries.title: Prompting Rule: Say Only What Matters
entries.body:
If it is important to the shot, write it clearly. If it is not important, do not add it just to make the prompt longer.

Simple shot (one person sitting and speaking): a short prompt is enough.
Detailed shot (camera moves + dialogue + object interaction + timing + reaction): many variables must happen in order, so more explicit instructions reduce ambiguity.

Write as much as the shot needs, not as much as possible.

entries.title: Realism Checklist
entries.body:
- Natural skin texture.
- Realistic fabric, glass, metal, walls, roads and other materials.
- Lighting that belongs to the location and time of day.
- Natural depth between foreground, subject and background.
- Small imperfections instead of perfect surfaces everywhere.
- Simple, believable body movement.
- Objects having weight and interacting correctly with the environment.
- Avoiding unnecessary visual effects.

The test: "Could a real camera have captured this?"

entries.title: Reference Video Jobs
entries.body:
Tell the model which axis of the reference matters:
- World continuity: same set construction, lighting logic, atmosphere, production quality
- Action energy: same event still in progress, same intensity and physical weight
- Camera character: same cinematic register, operator presence, overall quality
- Voice + performance: same vocal character, delivery register, energy

Prompt wins on action; reference wins on texture and world feel. Pair with an image reference when character identity matters.

entries.title: Scene Understanding Questions
entries.body:
For each scene, ask:
- Who is there?
- Where are they?
- What is happening?
- What does the audience need to understand?
- What is the most important action?
- What should the audience notice?
- What is the emotional tone?
- What needs to match the next or previous shot?

Then split into visual moments: one visual moment = one thing the audience needs to see.

entries.title: Script to Video Workflow
entries.body:
SCRIPT → UNDERSTAND THE SCENE → CAST THE CHARACTERS → MAKE CHARACTER SHEETS → IDENTIFY LOCATIONS / OBJECTS → BREAK THE STORY INTO VISUAL MOMENTS → DECIDE WHAT EACH SHOT SHOULD SHOW → WRITE THE PROMPT → GENERATE → CHECK → FIX → EDIT

Use the character reference for casting and identity; explain the rest (location, action, camera, lighting, dialogue, movement) directly in the prompt. The generated visuals replace a traditional storyboard.

entries.title: MCSLA Video Prompt
entries.notes: Five layers: Model · Camera · Subject · Look · Action. Keep under ~200 words.
entries.body:
Model: [model name]. Aspect ratio [16:9], duration [8s].
Camera: [one named camera move or shot size + angle].
Subject: {{subject}}
Look: [style, lighting, color grade].
Action: [one clear physical action, then the end state].

entries.title: Physical Action Template
entries.notes: Answer: what causes the movement, which direction, what it touches, where it ends, does the character react, what should NOT happen.
entries.body: {{subject}} is affected by [CAUSE]. It slowly moves [DIRECTION]. It touches [CONTACT POINT], then moves to [FINAL POSITION]. The movement follows natural gravity and realistic physics. The object must not [COMMON WRONG MOVEMENTS]. The character reacts [REACTION].

entries.title: Product Hero Shot
entries.body: {{subject}} on a seamless reflective surface, centered, clean studio softbox lighting with a subtle rim light, crisp specular highlights, shallow depth of field, premium minimal advertising look.

entries.title: Scene Starter
entries.notes: Smallest useful skeleton: who, where, when, doing what. Add camera, light and style fragments from the composer.
entries.body: {{subject}}, in [location], [time of day], [one clear action].

entries.title: Seedance 15s Three-Shot Block
entries.notes: A block needs a clear beginning, one main action and a clear end state. Too many unrelated actions → split into more blocks.
entries.body:
15-second continuous sequence with three connected shots.

SHOT 1 — 0-5 seconds
[Beat 1: establishing or detail. Subject: {{subject}}. Camera start, move and framing.]

SHOT 2 — 5-10 seconds
[Beat 2: main action. What stays sharp, what is out of focus, how the camera moves.]

SHOT 3 — 10-15 seconds
[Beat 3: reaction or information. Dialogue if any. Clear end state that can connect to the next block.]

Keep the same character, location, lighting and props throughout. [Realism notes.] [Restrictions.]

entries.title: Seedance Practical Prompt Order
entries.notes: Not a fixed formula — the order to think through when you need control. Write what matters, skip the rest.
entries.body:
[Duration / shot type].
[Location and time of day].
[Character + character reference]: {{subject}}
[Appearance / costume if relevant].
[Action — exactly what the character does].
[Camera movement and framing — where it starts, what it sees, how it moves].
[Important timing or physical action — what happens at which second].
[Lighting that fits the scene].
[Audio / dialogue if needed — what is said and when].
[Performance — how the character behaves].
[Visual style / realism].
[What must not happen: no cuts, no extra characters, no identity change].

entries.title: Single-Character Position Prompt
entries.notes: For one character where position, pose and contact points matter. For two or more characters, anchor cross-character geometry separately.
entries.body:
[At/from N seconds] One character in frame.

[Identity, Soul ID handle].
  Screen position: [left third / center / right third], x-position [%], y-position [%], frame occupancy [%].
  Depth layer: [foreground / midground / background].
  Body orientation: [toward camera / away / profile-left / profile-right / three-quarter].
  Pose: [physical configuration].
  Gaze: [where they look — frame-position or off-screen direction].
  Contact points: [physical surfaces — feet planted, hand on doorframe].
  State lock: [emotional or physical state].

One dominant action: [single action — one motion verb at the spine of the shot].
Motion: [secondary motion — hair, fabric, breath; eye motion].

Camera: [shot size], [angle], [lens], [movement — one dominant motion].
Setting: [location, time, weather, atmosphere].
Aesthetic: [genre, lighting, color grade, texture].
Audio: [ambience, SFX, dialogue, music].
Final frame: [composition at last frame].
